I'm a human factors grad student with a background in health informatics, computer science, and machine learning. 

Looking for 1-2 teammates with web dev, data visualization, or AI/ML skills :)
summary:
Astronauts get headaches on the ISS at CO2 levels that ground testing says should be fine. Part of the reason is that nothing records what a crew member breathed and how they felt on the same timeline.

Cabin sensors read the whole module so the air right at someone’s face can be much worse while the panel still says everything is normal. NASA has already tested personal CO2 monitors on crew, so the measurement exists. The gap is the person.

CO2zy is a working app that fills it in. You say one sentence about how you feel, it turns that into tagged symptoms, and it lines them up against the CO2 measured near your face over the previous ten hours. You get your week on one timeline, a likely reason your headache keeps happening, and something to actually do about it. It also writes a short summary for the flight surgeon and exports data where every check-in is already matched to the exposure that came before it.

It does not predict symptoms and it does not diagnose. It builds the record that would let someone study the link.

We built it in two days, tested it with three users, and fixed it based on the user feedback.
details:
CO2zy has four screens built around the three things this challenge asks for: gather, evaluate, act.

Now screen shows how much CO2 is in the air right at your face, next to the cabin average, so you can see the gap a wall sensor misses. If it is elevated, it gives you three specific things to try: check your crew quarters fan intake, move to a better ventilated module, flag it for the flight surgeon. Check in screen lets you report how you feel by talking or typing one sentence, something like “woke up with a headache again slept badly.” The app pulls out the symptoms and a severity level and you correct anything it got wrong before saving. Me screen puts your whole week on one timeline, each day a colored bar and each check-in a circle sitting on the hour it happened. Brief screen writes a short summary for a flight surgeon and exports a spreadsheet where every check-in already has the exposure that preceded it attached.

Each check-in gets paired with a ten hour look-back window, long enough to cover a full night of sleep, and we report the peak, the average, and how many minutes were spent above threshold. We flag long build-ups by comparing readings to each person’s own calm baseline rather than a fixed cutoff, using a higher bar to start an episode than to end one so a single noisy reading does not create a false alarm. What counts as high is different for different people, which is the point the research kept making.

We got to the solution by reading first. We found that scrubbers and ventilation already handle cabin air, and personal CO2 monitors have already been flown and tested. However, the link between the two was missing. Crew report CO2 symptoms below what ground testing predicts, fixed sensors can miss local fluctuations, and in microgravity there is no buoyant convection to carry exhaled CO2 away from a sleeping person’s face. This sits inside NASA’s hostile closed environment hazard and none of it gets solved by better hardware. It gets solved by a better record, which is a software problem.

CO2zy is structured as an exposure and symptom record, with breathing-zone CO2 as the first indicator. Sleep hours and mood are already captured in the check-in.

We use AI in three places: turning speech and free text into structured symptoms, spotting build-ups in the sensor stream, and drafting the flight surgeon summary. We deliberately do not use it to predict symptoms. There is nowhere near enough symptom data for that, and a confident prediction built on thin data would be worse than no prediction. The AI works on the plentiful items, sensors and language, and stays away from the scarce items, which is how people actually felt. The user also reviews and is able to edit everything the AI pulls out before it is saved.

It is built in React and JavaScript with Vite. Every visual, including the exposure timeline, the animated breathing zone halo and the entire icon set, is hand-written SVG with no charting or icon libraries, so the app loads fast and has almost no dependencies. Data persists in browser storage. We wrote it in VS Code on macOS and deployed it as a static site and it runs in any phone browser today. The simulated sensor feed enters the app at a single point, so a real CO2 sensor would plug into the same place without changing anything downstream.

We tested it with three people who had never seen it, timing five tasks each and taking a 5-Likert scale easiness rating after every one. All 15 tasks were completed with zero errors, median time on task was 16.3 seconds, and mean ease was 4.1 out of 5. The useful part was where it went badly. The lowest rated task (3 out of 5) was finding whether their headaches lined up with high CO2 nights, which is the one thing the whole app exists to do. Everyone completed it, nobody made an error, but nobody felt it was easy. The feedback we got about that is that the timeline had no axis labels or legend, so they could not tell what the colors or the circles meant, and the scale ran green to red, which is unreadable with red-green color blindness. We rebuilt it. The scale is now blue, yellow, orange and rose, the two most severe levels carry diagonal hatching so severity survives grayscale and full color blindness, the legend states the mmHg range for every band, the check-in circles came off the color scale entirely and now use size for severity, and both axes are labeled. Logging a check-in also ran longer than we designed for, 31.7 seconds median against the ten we were aiming at, though that includes reading the screen for the first time. Shortening the first run is the next fix.

What we hope to achieve is that crew members get a visible reason for a symptom and a specific action instead of a vague complaint. A flight surgeon gets a time-stamped record instead of a recollection from someone who has been awake for twenty hours. A researcher gets the first dataset that pairs individual exposure with individual symptoms in a format that can be compared across missions, which is what would eventually be needed to answer the question that started all of this. Furthermore, it is the same pattern HRP uses for Standard Measures, applied to environmental exposure.

On Earth it is the same problem with a wider reach. For instance, classrooms, offices, clinics and submarines, anywhere people sit in a sealed room, feel bad, and think the air is fine because the one sensor on the wall says so.

This project contains limitations. The sensor data in this version is simulated. A reading from one of those is an estimate of the air around you, not the CO2 in your blood. A week of data from one person is a pattern, not proof, and sleep, workload and hydration all affect how someone feels. The app says so on screen where a user would otherwise over-read it. Nothing here is a medical device and nothing here diagnoses.
